Copper Long-term Outlook 

# Executive summary 

2011 turned out to be slightly softer than suggested in our previous report.  Although full year data is not as yet finalised, it is clear that the impact of the European debt crisis and the prevailing cool wind of sentiment led to weaker consumption growth across the globe, and in particular Asia outside China.  The net result has been to lower global demand growth in 2011 to 2.7% from 3.7% in the December 2011 LTO report.  Meanwhile, the nascent improvement in Europe and the US remains encouraging for global demand prospects in 2012.  This has led us to revise our refined consumption for the USA higher in 2012 as prospects for semis production has been supported to some extent by recent macro economic data, even from the long-suffering housing and construction sector.  Although Chinese buyers failed to return to the market post Chinese New Year, the premature stock build from large scale Chinese cathode imports in Q4 2011 will support refined growth this year and thus our outlook for China in 2012 is unchanged.  For the year as a whole we forecast global demand growth of 3.7%, and 3.5% on average through our forecast period. 

Disruptions were once again a key factor to the low outturn for refined production in 2011, with strikes, technical failures and low ore grades the key contributors to output of 19.968Mt, slightly higher than the 19.694Mt in our Q4 report.  A combination of lower production and demand in 2011, led to a supply shortfall of just 93kt for the copper market, and while much smaller than the 257kt deficit in 2010, this squeezed stocks lower to 54 days of consumption by the year end, to keep prices supported as we headed into 2012.  Prices were on average 17% higher in 2011 at $8810/t ($4.00lb) on 2010 average copper prices of $7536/t ($3.42lb). 

Overall base case mine production capability is forecast to decline by 0.5% p.a. between 2011 and 2025 due to resource depletion with output falling from a peak of ~20.66Mt in 2015 to just under 15Mt in 2025.  In 2011, demand for mine production exceeded available base case supply by c.300kt, lower than our Q4 estimate of almost 400kt but within the range of analysis over the course of this year.  We expect the market to move closer to balance this year of c.180kt, while material from projects under construction will likely push the market into surplus in 2013 and 2014. 

Our smelter production estimate for 2011 now stands at 15.5M

t which is 5.1% higher than was the case in 2010.  This year and next, we expect smelter output to show even stronger growth at 8.5% and 7.9%, respectively, as higher mine feed filters through for onward processing.  Overall, we expect 4.8Mt/a of additional smelting output over the forecast period, with 2.9Mt of this coming from developments in China. 

The majority of the revisions made to our smelter production capability forecasts are largely reflected in the changes to our refinery output estimates and these can be seen in the main report.  Taking these into account, base case global copper refined production reached 19.7Mt/a in 2011 (+3.6%), while capability is expected to increase by a substantial 9.6% this year, to 21.6Mt.  A further 9% year-on-year increment in 2013 will see this figure rise to 23.5Mt/a in 2013, and then to 24.8Mt in 2014.  However, growth is forecast to slow markedly in 2015, and then to decline from 2016 onwards. As a consequence, overall global capability will increase by only 1.4% p.a. between 2010 and 2025.  In tonnage terms this equates to an increase of ~4.37Mt to 23.38Mt in 2025. 

We remain of the view that 2012 will record its third consecutive year of global deficit in the copper market of ~150kt. Growth in refined production of 3.4% will lag that of consumption to push metal stocks days of consumption lower to just 49 days compared to 54 days in 2011.  We expect 2012 prices to remain supported above $8500/t over the remaining three quarters, as the premature stock build from large scale Chinese cathode imports in Q4 2011 softened some of the anticipated price impact from the market in Q1 2012.  We are of the opinion that Chinese demand improvements will be centred on the second half of the year and it is for this reason that we now project prices to peak in the third quarter and to average close to $9,000/t to reflect tightness in the market, with full year prices to average $8580/t ($3.89/lb) in 2011$. 2013 will be the peak year for growth in both mine and refined copper production which will push the market into a fullyfledged surplus of 565kt, even as refined consumption benefits from an improving macro-economic environment.  As supply growth exceeds that of demand and metals stocks advance to average 57 days we expect to see prices come under pressure and now forecast 2013 prices to average $7880/t ($3.57/lb) in 2011$. 

Copper prices will ease in 2014 and 2015 as they surrender to the surpluses that are set to emerge and as metal stocks days to consumption build to 66 days.  A balanced market in 2016 will see prices recover to average $6834/t ($3.10/lb) in 2011$, although as the surpluses build over the next few years and stocks reach 70 days, prices are expected to slide to a low in 2018 of $6063/t ($2.75/lb) in 2011$.  The declining prices and emerging surpluses of the prior years will dampen new project and/or expansion investment and lead to weaker production growth in 2019 and 2020, nudging the marke

t closer to balance of ~ 70kt and a short lived deficit ~180kt, respectively. This will come around the same time as a projected global economic recovery, which will encourage higher prices of $6173-6614/t ($2.80-3.00/lb) in constant 2011$ over the period 2019-2020. Our long-term incentive price has been increased to $3.00/lb in current dollars over the period to 2025 as miners continue to experience increases in operating and capital costs over and above general inflation. This has been derived from our analysis of mine project incentive prices and projected demand for mine production over this period. However, there would typically be an upturn in demand from March onwards, although this h

as failed to materialise this year.  Somewhat ironically, the strength of imports at the start of the year is overstating apparent consumption, which is the opposite of a year ago when destocking amid record high prices were understating real demand.  We remain of the opinion that consumption will begin to pick up from the second quarter and that overall growth will be focussed on the second half of the year, while we reiterate our expectation of an 8% expansion this year.  Demand will then edge lower in both the near and longer term, with growth of 7% forecast on average through the period 2011 to 2016, before slowing further still to 4.8% on average through the remainder of the forecast period. 

**Investment to boost electrical sector in 2012** One of the key reasons we remain relatively bullish on prospects for demand this year is our expectation of a rebound in infrastructure spending, which will drive the electrical sector.  We have noted previously that the build out of energy networks will support demand for some time in China as grid improvements take place but this year given expectations of a slowdown in the economy investment is set to expand to support activity.  In fact, comments from the State Council suggest that state led infrastructure investment may grow by 15-20% this year, a rate not seen since 2010.  In 2013 growth will likely be scaled back, however, we still anticipate solid support from this sector right through our forecast period as Chinese power generation struggles to keep pace with economic development. 

**Construction slowdown likely to come in 2013** A slowdown in the construction sector in China this year has been engineered by the government as it bids to slowdown house price inflation and to dampen a speculative bubble.  This is proving to be relatively effective, although the downside is the expected negative impact on copper demand.  However, it is worth noting that copper is typically used towards the end of a build and as such, a slowdown in new building this year is more likely to impact demand for copper next year.  As such, we are not expecting a dramatic slowdown in consumption from this sector this year, although question marks remain over the outlook for 2013.  Further out, we expect construction within the tier 2 and tier 3 cities to support sectoral growth through the forecast period. 

**Increasing Cu content to support autos demand through forecast period** The automotive market has endured a sluggish start to 2012 although we still forecast an improvement on the lacklustre pace of growth in 2011.  Last year was always expected to be a year of consolidation for the Chinese automotive market following the stellar growth of the previous two years and indeed, total vehicle production rose by a modest 1% to 18.4 million units.  For 2012, however, we forecast a rebound in production of c.7%, with similar growth expected in 2013 and 2014 and while we anticipate

Copper Long-term Outlook 

## Europe 

**Re-stocking provides first quarter boost** The sharp contraction in demand in the final part of 2011 was in part driven by de-stocking across supply chains as firms adopted a wait and see attitude amid economic uncertainty.  While the major stumbling blocks to resolving the euro debt crisis appear to have been mostly resolved it is probably a little premature to declare an outright end to the currency group’s troubles.  Significantly, businesses across the region, although most notably in Germany, seem to be placing orders again and this has led to an improvement in demand for copper in the first quarter of this year.  It is too early to state with any conviction whether this represents a recovery in consumption or that the upturn was simply re-stocking activity, although semis producers do feel a lot more upbeat about demand conditions. 

**Economic weakness to weigh on full year demand** The better near term demand conditions are not immediately obvious from our industrial production forecasts, which for much of Europe point to a contraction in output.  Indeed, Germany, France, Italy and Spain will all experience a decline in activity this year and even by 2013 we are still only forecasting growth of c.1% for these countries.  The negative industrial and economic backdrop will cast a dark pale over demand for copper and as such, we forecast negative growth in regional demand this year, with only a modest improvement in 2013.  The improvement in industrial output in the following two years will then result in a cyclical peak in consumption.  For the period 2011 to 2016 we forecast average annual growth of c.2%, which will then slow to leave little or no growth on average out to 2025. 

**Aurubis in further downstream rationalisation** Aurubis has announced its intention to close its copper semis plant at Yverdon-Les-Bains in Switzerland as it seeks to streamline operations.  Output of around 4kt per year of complex profiles will be transferred to Olen in Belgium, where production of profiles will be focussed.  This rationalisation follows on from Aurubis announcing late last year that it is to close its semis plant at Finspang in Sweden. 

**Italian semis output down by 5% in 2011** Italian semis output fell away sharply in the fourth quarter of the year as demand ground to a halt.  Indeed, copper semis production fell by 12.1% year on year in the fourth quarter, while copper alloy semis output declined by a similar 12.2%.  This resulted in a full year contraction overall of 4.8% in semis including alloys in Italy in 2011 following the 18.6% expansion in 2010.  For 2012 we expect It

alian demand to contract a further 1- 2%. 

**Russia to ease back after tax induced surge** As we noted on a number of occasions during the past year, Russian apparent consumption of copper surged in 2011 as a result of the reintroduction of a tax on cathode at the start of that year.  The result was that rather than export refined copper, material was processed at home into wire rod, which was often then exported but this resulted in a massive increase in domestic consumption of refined copper even if the final product was then shipped abroad.  However, for this year we expect there to be a bit of a hangover in Russia as export markets for wire rod flag.  Growth in demand in 2011 was a lofty 59% but we foresee a decline of c.2% this year. 

**Construction set for continued weakness** The Euro construction orders PMI was 42.2 in January – an improvement from December’s 39.6 but still reflecting sharp falls in construction order books within the euro area.  The data showed declining activity in all of the residential, commercial and civil sectors, but the civil sector looks particularly bad, as austerity measures across Europe result in falling government investment.  The commercial activity index was 44.3, indicating that businesses remain reluctant to invest in the current economic climate.  In all, total construction in the euro area will almost certainly decline again in 2012, making it the fifth straight year of contraction.  Further out conditions do not look much better either, with no more than 1% growth on average in construction activity expected right through to 2025. 

**Electrical sector dented by solar weakness** Changes to feed in tariffs in Germany are leading to short term weakness in the solar segment of the electrical sector and this is tempering demand from what has been a red hot sector.  After rampant growth over the past few years boosted by generous feed in tariffs, these have now been cut by around 30% and this is likely to hit sectoral growth in the short term.  The growth of this sector has attracted a lot of competition from solar cell producers and rationalisation is probably required before the next stage of growth can take place.  However, the longer term prospects remain healthy for green energy, particularly as nuclear power is becoming increasingly unpalatable. 

**Indicators pointing east for transport growth** The motor vehicle market is set to face a period of consolidation or even retrenchment this year after the sharp growth of 2010 and 2011.  In relatively uncertain economic times consumers are putting off purchases of vehicles and as such, production will also be hit, which explains our forecast of overall European vehicle production showing little to no growth in 2012.  The following years should see some improvement across the region but over the longer term growth will be focussed on eastern Europe, with Russia and Poland in particular enjoying strong growth.  Set against production forecasts we also nee

d to consider the average copper content of vehicles and how this is expected to change in order to get to final sectoral consumption. Given an expected increase in penetration of hybrid and electric vehicles over our forecast period, in addition to increases in copper usage as cars become more complex, we expect steady growth in demand from the motor vehicle sector. Even if there are some tentative signs of improvement in the US and European economies, it would be more than a little premature to point to a decisive upswing, while the strength of the yen is not only hurting exports in the short run it is also posing a question mark over their longer term viability. Indeed, not only are Japanese manufacturers considering the future location of their production facilities but so are semis producers. It is worth noting that industrial production is still below pre-quake levels in Japan and while output will undoubtedly swing back above the year ago level in March the economy still has a long way to go before returning to pre economic crisis levels. In fact, according to our forecasts, industrial output will not return to the levels seen in 2007 until around 2015 to 2016. **Competing trends to affect Japanese demand** The recovery that we forecast for the Japanese economy will certainly find its way into demand for copper although not necessarily in such a direct manner as might be expected. Indeed, there are many divergent trends in end use markets, with some of these positive for demand but some less so. For example, the largest sector, electrical and electronic products faces severe headwinds from a retrenchment in investment from power companies in the sh

ort term. However, transport markets are recovering from the disruption from last year while construction is expected to post at least some improvement. Overall, these should net each other off to some extent but leave demand up c.2% in 2012. Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - March 2012 Page 9 of 32 Copper Long-term Outlook **Electrical sector lacks spark in short term** The key electrical and electronics sector has been dealt a heavy blow by the nuclear disaster which has resulted in energy producers scaling back investment as they deal with the closure of nuclear power stations. This is hitting demand for copper products from the sector in the short term, although this ought to at least provide a boost to demand, possibly from 2014 onwards as deferred investment takes place. At the same time, demand for electronic products is being hit by weakness in key export markets, although this too should stage a recovery in line with global economic activity over the next few years. In particular, demand for copper foil is flagging presently across key electronics markets, with demand from Lithium Ion batteries for cars the one bright spot in the short term. **Construction faces negative headwinds** The long term decline of the Japanese construction market may be interrupted by a blip upwards over the next year or so as reconstruction efforts temporarily provide a boost to demand but even this will only be relatively modest. In fact, after enjoying something of an improvement through the middle of last year, housing starts are now on the wane again, having posted five consecutive year-on-year declines through to January of this year. As such, there is no major reason to look to this sector to support demand growth over the longer term. **Hybrid and electric vehicles set to temper declining auto production** The automotive market is unarguably the bright spot in the Japanese market as production of automobiles recovers from the disruptions of the previous year. Those disruptions are well documented but the key point is that car production fell by 13.9% last year, although is set to recover strongly in 2012, expanding at a similar rate to leave 2012

output just a little shy of 2010 production. The following year should see further growth but thereafter we forecast that producers will continue to shift car plants overseas to lower cost locations, which will result in a gradual decline in domestic auto output. Demand from the sector will follow a similar pattern, however, against the backdrop of declining output will be increased average copper content of vehicles. Last year’s mine growth of 0.7% continued the meager year-on-year improvement that we have been accustomed to seeing for most of the past decade.  The brighter areas of Africa (+5.6%), China (+9.4%), North America (+5.9%) and Oceania (+6.5%) were outweighed by a massive 17.7% drop in Asia and stagnation (-0.2%) in Latin America.  This year’s potential mined copper output figure of c.17.75Mt globally reflects growth across virtually all geographic areas, with Africa’s 20%+ year-on-year improvement and a near 12% surge from Latin America off

setting the sole anticipated area of stagnation, which is Asia (-0.4%). Strike action at Freeport’s Grasberg in Indonesia during May and between September and December last year was the main contributor to Asia’s poor 2011 performance, and a slow start to 2012, plus continued exposure to low grade areas, will hinder this year’s output. Despite this, 2012 should be the first of three consecutive years averaging nearly 8% annual mine production growth, something which has not been seen since the mid-1990s. This growth rate can be seen in our “base case” alone. Although we expect there to be virtually no further contribution from advanced-stage projects this year, we do have a total of c.175kt additional copper coming from “highly probable” and “probable” projects in 2013, and a further 460kt metal in 2014. Even though we would not expect all these new copper units to come on stream in a timely fashion, the base case scenario + project expectation lend greater confidence of a stronger response from the supply side than we have seen in recent memory. The downside, of course, is that this surge in output should push the market into the anticipated surplus over the same period. Even so, over the long term base case mine output will decline through attrition to 18.6Mt by 2020 and to 15Mt by 2025, representing an annual 0.5% loss in tonnage terms. New scrap, or manufacturing scrap, is generated during the fabrication of copper products and returned to the mill for reprocessing, or sold, and is not considered a new source of copper supply. A manufacturer may generate up to 60% of scrap as clippings, trimmings, stampings, borings, and turnings when processing copper and copper-base products into finished articles. New scrap is termed "run-around" or home scrap (which does not enter the scrap statistics) when it is generated internally at the plant re-using it, or it may be called "purchased return scrap" when returned by a customer from a plant external to that purchasing and re-using it. Old scrap is generated from worn out, discarded or obsolete copper products and thus, is considered to be a “new” source of supply. ## Scrapping rates The availability of _old_ copper scrap is linked to the volume of copper-containing products installed/purchased and their life cycles, or duration. The life of copper in electrical equipment and machinery averages 30-35 years; in non-electrical machinery, 15 years; in housing, 35-75 years; in transportation, 10 years; in all other sectors, about 10 years. The average for the industry is estimated to be 15-20 years. The rate of (old) scrap recovery and its availability to be the market is limited not only by copper's long life, but also by the sensitivity of scrap collection rates to market prices. Over the past 20 years, the volume of _new_ copper scrap has not grown in line with industrial consumption of copper because manufacturing efficiencies have improved, leading to as much as a 50% fall in new scrap generation over the period. ## Scrap usage Most old scrap recovered from the market place must be reprocessed either by smelting and refining, or, to a lesser extent, by leaching and electrowinning to form a pure copper product. Fire refining in a reverberatory or other furnace may be sufficient for the better grades of scrap. This latter process uses oxidation, fluxing and reduction, with a refined ingot, wire bar, slab, or billet usually being the end product. Certain products, such as brass rod (manufactured using 80-90% scrap) can contain higher amounts of scrap than others while still maintaining prod

uct quality tolerance.  Others, such as wire rod, must contain far less impurities (typically 5%) since these could affect the drawability (leading to snapping) of the wire rod in producing wire.  New scrap is readily used by brass and copper tube mills to generate new semi-fabricated forms with little additional treatment. Because minimal clean-up procedures are needed, this type of scrap is commonly called "direct melt", or No.1 scrap.  In general, No. 1 scrap is contained in copper and copper-alloy products, rather than wire rod.  Scrap purchases by brass mills are based primarily on activity levels at the mills and the relative price differential between cathode and No. 1 scrap, rather than the actual copper price.  When business conditions are strong, brass mills have access to large volumes of return scrap.  When manufacturing (and, possibly imports) decline, mills may be forced to increase their cathode purchases. 

Low copper prices over the period 1997-2003 led to a reduction in the availability of smelting and refining grade scrap with a corresponding decline in the processing of this material in countries such the USA and in Europe.  The notable exception has been China where there has been an upward trend in the treatment of smelting and refining grade scrap material.  Economic and environmental considerations have also played a major role, with the cost of environmental compliance often leading to plant closures, particularly in the USA.  This is despite the fact that the cost of recovering one tonne of copper from scrap is approximately half that of recovery through the conventional route (concentratesmelting-refining).  Secondary smelters and ingot markers typically consume the lion's share (90%) of No.2 scrap and most of the auto radiators and red brass scrap.

Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - March 2012 Page 29 of 32 Copper Long-term Outlook # Principle uses of copper Copper consumption can be divided into three main product groups which are copper wire rod, copper products and copper alloy products. Copper wire rod, which accounts for an estimated 55% of total Global consumption (i.e. including scrap) and ~70% of primary consumption, is copper’s main first use. With the exception of silver, copper has the highest electrical conductivity of all the metals. This helps to explain why the principal application for copper wire rod is wire and cable. Wire rod is consumed in five main wire and cable markets which include general and industrial cable, utility power cable, telecommunication cable, other insulated wire and winding wire. In general, wire and cable and copper products are consumed in five broad sectors: construction, electric and electronic products, industrial machinery

and equipment, transportation equipment and consumer and general products.  Of these, construction is the largest sector for consuming copper, accounting for 33% of total copper consumption.  The main wire and cable and copper products consumed in the construction industry include building wire, power cable, copper plumbing and air conditioning tube, copper sheet and alloy products. 

Building wire is the largest of the wire and cable markets, accounting for ~35% of wire rod consumption.  Rising intensity of use, in both the mature and developing economies, will be largely responsible for building wire maintaining this position.  The number of electrical appliances used at home and at the workplace continues to rise, particularly in the mature economies, thereby leading to an increase in the number of power outlets needed per building.  In addition, recent technical issues imply that more copper wire and cable will be needed in the future.  One of these issues, electrical energy efficiency involves using less power to perform a given task by using more or heavier copper conductors.  Finally, good power quality, defined as the uninterrupted, undistorted flow of electricity at the correct voltage, is also helping to drive up the demand for building wire due to higher power quality being achieved by installing additional circuits and heavier wires and cables. 

In contrast to the building and industrial cable market, the power utility market is the smallest of all the wire and cable segments.  However, demand growth for power cable will be supported by both the general recovery in utility investment and the fact that copper, the mainstay of power grids worldwide, still has considerable potential to carry energy better and reduce losses than aluminium. 

Copper tube, which accounts for an estimated 13% of global refined copper consumption, is the largest of the copper product markets.  The two main uses are in plumbing and heating systems and in air conditioners and refrigeration (ACR tube).  The steady proliferation of plumbing amenities in and around the home, particularly as many houses built today within the mature economies have more than one bathroom, are largely responsible for copper plumbing tube demand growth, however, this is being offset by substitution to plastic tubing where this is possible.  Elsewhere, improved living standards in the developing economies, leading to higher demand for air conditioners, continues to boost demand for ACR tube.  This is particularly the case in China and India where improved power supply will lead to a surge in the consumption of air conditioners over the coming years.  Meanwhile in the mature economies, the market is being driven by external factors such as environmental issues, regulatory concerns and social demands for comfort. 

Other copper and copper alloy products consumed by the construction sector include copper sheet and strip, rods, bars and sections plus brass products.  Copper sheet is used

for roofing, eaves gutters, drain pipes for rainwater and lining for facades, while rods bars and sections, along with brass products, are used for building fixture and fittings.  In hospitals, brass doorknobs and push plates are widely used because it has been proven that they help to reduce cross contamination. 

Electrical and electronic products are copper’s second largest consuming sector, accounting for 33% of total copper demand.  Copper containing electrical and electronic products include telecommunication cable, power cable, transformer windings, semiconductors and motors for heavy appliances. 

Since the early 1990s copper telecommunication cable has been largely substituted by fibre optic cable in long distance networks.  However, copper telecom cable has remained the preferred link between the main network and consumers. In addition, the development of the internet and e-mail has further enhanced the role of copper in telecommunications in recent years.  The need for information to be carried more quickly along the telecommunication network has led to the introduction of asymmetrical digital subscriber line technology (ADSL).  The ADSL is a dedicated circuit between a home and the telephone company’s central office that uses normal copper telephone lines.  The addition of an ADSL chip to the existing copper network means that users can download files around 15 times faster than an analogue dial-up connection. 

Dramatic gains in copper consumption to have occurred within the home because of a system known to the telecommunications industry as ‘structured wiring’.  The cable carrying voice, computer and television signals is connected to a central hub in the home.  Individual cables then run independently from here to high-quality connections in rooms throughout the house.  Cables connected to the hub consist of four pairs of twisted wires, capable of carrying more electronic signals with less interference and resistance than the older four-stranded telephone wires. her main wire and cable segment to supply the electrical sector is winding wire.  Winding wire demand accounts for an estimated 20% of copper wire rod consumption, making it the third largest wire and cable market.  Applications include transformers, generators, stereos, television sets and motors.  Indeed, it is the need to improve electrical efficiency of this last application, particularly in the mature economies, that has generated the most growth in winding wire demand recently.  This is because improved electrical efficiency involves using a larger conductor in order to reduce electrical resistance, as well as ensuring that the proper voltages are delivered when needed.  In addition, the efficiency of electric motors is being improved further by introducing copper into the rotor as opposed to aluminium.  Meanwhile, in the developing economies, demand growth will mainly stem from increased consumption of electrical goods as disposable incomes rise. 

Copper’s third largest consuming sector, industrial machinery and equipment, accounts for 13% of total consumption. Both copper wire and cable and semi products supply this sector which includes equipment and machinery, industrial valves and fittings, off-highway vehicles and heat exchangers.  Copper wire and copper and copper alloy products are also used in transportation equipment, copper’s fourth largest category.  This includes the automotive, marine and aircraft/aerospace sectors.  It is within the automotive sector that developments of new copper applications have been most concentrated in recent years.  Prior to 1930, copper and brass, having excellent pressure containing and anticorrosion characteristics, were the favoured materials to be used in brake tubing.  However, mass auto production in the 1940s led to the adoption of furnace-brazed steel tubing because it was much lower in cost.  Although this form of tubing is still widely used today, copper has re-gained some of its lost market share through the introduction of a copper-nickel alloy (90% copper/10% nickel) which is more resistant to corrosion from road mud and salt than steel piping.  Likewise, new technology has led to the development of a new brazed copper-brass automotive radiator which has the necessary requirements to recapture some of the market share displaced by aluminium over the past twenty years. 

Meanwhile, 42-volt systems, hybrid vehicles and numerous electrical and electronic applications provide additional growth prospects for the use of copper within the automotive sector Over the years the number of electrical and electronic components installed per unit has been rising steadily, thereby creating the need for growth in the power and signal distribution system (otherwise known as the wiring harness).  Many of the electrical components will have to be redesigned in order to work effectively with the higher-voltage systems which could result in the copper content of some of the electrical components falling, but

as more power becomes available, new electrical components will emerge. Such examples include electronic valve actuation and electric braking, resulting in several kilos of copper, per unit, being added. Meanwhile, the introduction of electric and hybrid vehicles will also increase demand for copper from this sector as they typically have a much higher copper content than traditional vehicles because of the amount of copper in batteries among other components. Forecasts have shown that over the next ten years, increases per vehicle will outweigh the decreases in copper required per component. Copper’s final end-use category is consumer and general products. Copper consumed in this sector accounts for 8% of total copper consumption. The three main end-uses are electrical appliances, military ordnance and coinage. The production of the Euro coin in recent years has helped to support demand for copper and copper alloy products.
